readingInstruction: Read Psalm 117, the shortest chapter in the Bible. Paul quotes it in Romans 15:11 at the climax of his argument that the gospel unites Jew and Gentile. You have read this psalm before. Read it today as part of Paul’s closing argument in Romans.
settingTheScene: Psalm 117 sits at the center of the Bible in the Hebrew-English Bible’s order of chapters, at the end of the Hallel’s first half. In just two verses it calls all nations to praise the LORD. Paul will use it in Romans 15 as the proof text that the Gentiles were always meant to glorify God for his mercy. Reading it in the middle of Romans, as we approach the practical chapters, we see the goal of the letter: a united people of Jew and Gentile worshiping one God.
interpretation:
The psalm contains one command and one reason. The command: “Praise the LORD, all nations! Extol him, all peoples!” The reason: “For great is his steadfast love toward us, and the faithfulness of the LORD endures forever.” Notice again that the reason for the nations to praise is God’s love “toward us,” toward Israel. This is the logic of Romans 9 to 11. God’s faithfulness to Israel is the means by which the nations learn to praise.

In Romans 15:8-9, Paul explains: “Christ became a servant to the circumcised to show God’s truthfulness, in order to confirm the promises given to the patriarchs, and in order that the Gentiles might glorify God for his mercy.” Two parts of one plan: Christ confirms the promises to Israel (God’s truthfulness), and the Gentiles glorify God for his mercy. Then Paul gathers four Old Testament quotations, from the Psalms, Deuteronomy, the Psalms again, and Isaiah, to prove that the Gentiles’ praise was always intended. Psalm 117:1 is the third of these: “Praise the Lord, all you Gentiles, and let all the peoples extol him.”

Notice how Psalm 117 brings together the two terms that have occupied us in Romans. “Steadfast love” is the word hesed, covenant mercy. “Faithfulness” is truth, reliability. These are God’s grace and truth, the two gifts that came through Jesus Christ (John 1:17). On the cross, steadfast love and faithfulness met. The nations are invited to praise because they, too, can now rest on God’s mercy.

The psalm is brief because the message is simple: the God of Israel is the God of all, and all should praise him. Short as it is, it carries the entire hope of the Bible. The scattered peoples of Babel will be brought together before the throne. Revelation 7:9 pictures “a great multitude that no one could number, from every nation, from all tribes and peoples and languages” praising God. This psalm is a first sketch of that scene.

Make it your own. When you praise the LORD in church, remember that you are joining a chorus drawn from every tribe, and the psalm is calling more to join.
connection: Romans 15:8-12 quotes this psalm with Psalm 18:49, Deuteronomy 32:43, and Isaiah 11:10. Genesis 12:3 promised blessing to all families of the earth. Psalm 67 and Psalm 96 also call the nations to praise. Isaiah 49:6 speaks of salvation to the end of the earth. John 1:17 says grace and truth came through Jesus Christ. Ephesians 2:11-22 says Jew and Gentile are one new man. Revelation 5:9 and 7:9-10 picture the nations in worship.
application:
Say the psalm aloud as a prayer. It takes about ten seconds.

Pray for the nations by name. Pick three countries and pray that they would praise the LORD.

Thank God that you are part of the people he has gathered from all the nations.
prayerPrompts: Praise the LORD with all the nations.
Thank him that Christ confirmed his promise to include them.
Pray for the nations to know him.
